body:
Calpers, the largest public pension fund in the United States, is carrying out a pronounced shift in its asset allocation. Based on calculations from regulatory filings, the fund cut the total number of shares it directly holds in the "Magnificent Seven" technology giants by 26% in the first half of 2026, while increasing its private equity position to reduce the risk of excessive concentration in public-market holdings.

Calpers Deputy Chief Investment Officer Anton Orlich said in an interview that valuations in the public equity market are at relatively elevated levels, and the heavy concentration of a handful of large companies in the indexes could weigh on relative returns. By contrast, pricing for private companies is more attractive, he said. He noted that increasing the private equity allocation helps provide a buffer when public markets weaken.

The reduction covers seven stocks: Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Nvidia, Meta and Tesla. Calpers' strategy is to convert large single holdings into a diversified model spread across hundreds of companies — essentially trading liquidity for risk diversification.

This pivot did not begin this year; it is the cumulative result of a series of strategic adjustments.

According to the fund's monthly report, as of September 30, 2026, Calpers had total assets of $651.3 billion, of which private equity accounted for an actual $145.6 billion, or 22.4%, and public equities $236.1 billion, or 36.3%. The private equity target ratio set by the Calpers board in March 2024 is 17%.

As of June 30, 2026, Calpers had assets under management of $637.1 billion (about NT$20.8 trillion), making it the largest pension fund for government employees in the United States. Data published by the fund in July showed a preliminary net investment return of 14.8% over the past 12 months, with strong performance in both public and private equity portfolios.

Note: Sources are calculations from regulatory filings and data published by the fund.

The logic behind this repositioning is not to chase last year's performance. Calpers' preliminary returns by asset class for fiscal 2025-26 (ended June 30) are as follows:

Real assets (real estate, infrastructure, etc.)

Note: Valuations for private markets (private equity, private credit, real assets) lag by one quarter and are as of March 31, 2026. The 24.1% return on public equities was actually higher than the 17.0% for private equity; Calpers' rationale for shifting toward private markets is its judgment on future valuations and concentration, not the relative performance of the past year.

In the same fiscal year, Calpers' funded status (assets relative to future benefit obligations) rose to 85% from 79% in the prior fiscal year, and the 14.8% return also exceeded the board's assumed long-term return of 6.8%, marking the best performance in five years.

Since July of this year, Calpers has implemented a "Total Portfolio Approach," a framework approved by the board in November 2025 that lets the investment team evaluate each strategy by its benefit to the fund as a whole rather than being constrained by fixed allocation weights for each asset class. Chief Investment Officer Stephen Gilmore said the fund will regularly and publicly measure whether active management is truly creating value for the fund, using a reference portfolio composed of 75% global equities and 25% U.S. Treasuries.

For Taiwanese readers, concentration is not a problem unique to the U.S. market. According to the constituent weights of the Taiwan Stock Exchange Capitalization Weighted Stock Index published by Taiwan Index Plus Corp., as of September 30, 2026, TSMC alone accounted for 41.12%. By comparison, the Magnificent Seven together account for about 35% of the S&P 500 (as of October 2026, per Motley Fool statistics). In other words, the Taiwanese stock market's dependence on a single company is even greater than the U.S. market's reliance on seven technology giants. The way large pension funds such as Calpers re-examine concentration and valuation is equally applicable to reviewing the risk structure of Taiwanese equity funds and index products.

It is worth noting that this repositioning occurred before U.S. technology stocks came under pressure. After several technology giants reported earnings this week, doubts intensified over whether artificial intelligence spending can translate into actual returns, and technology stocks saw concentrated selling; results from Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet are due next week, and the technology sector still faces further tests.

In terms of market impact, Calpers is enormous, and changes in its holdings are themselves a signal. Its high-profile retreat from the "Magnificent Seven" into private equity could prompt other large institutions to re-examine the concentration at the top of technology stocks and the logic of allocation amid high public-market valuations. For investors, it also means that after years of a technology bull market, large pension funds' assessment of the risk-return tradeoff has shifted.
